title: Two springs, one weight
hook: Hang a weight from two springs joined end to end. Stiffer than one spring, or stretchier?

knows: springs stretch more under a heavier weight
a 1 kg mass is pulled down with about 9.8 N
doesNotKnow: how springs combine in a chain and side by side

misconception: Two springs together are always stiffer than one.
objective: The learner can explain that in a chain each spring carries the whole weight and stretches as much as one spring alone, so the stretches add (twice as stretchy), while side by side they share the weight and each stretches half as much.

claims.text: Within its elastic range a spring stretches in proportion to the pull on it (Hooke's law, F = k x).
claims.source: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 7.1 (spring force F = -k x) and section 15.1.

claims.text: A 1 kg mass pulls down with 9.81 N; a spring that stretches 5 cm under it has stiffness 196 N/m.
Hung end to end, each spring carries the full 9.81 N and stretches 5 cm, so the mass drops 10 cm in total.
claims.source: Massless springs in series: the same force passes through each; x = 9.81 / 196.2 = 0.05 m each, total 0.10 m. Equivalent stiffness k/2 = 98.1 N/m (node).

claims.text: Side by side, each spring carries half the weight (4.91 N) and stretches 2.5 cm, so the mass drops 2.5 cm.
claims.source: Springs in parallel with a level bar: the load splits equally, 9.81 / 2 = 4.905 N each; x = 4.905 / 196.2 = 0.025 m. Equivalent stiffness 2k = 392 N/m (node).

claims.text: Idealisations: identical, weightless springs within their elastic range, and a light, level bar for the side-by-side rig.

recall.question: Three identical springs are hooked end to end under a weight that stretches one spring 4 cm. How far does the weight drop?
recall.why: In a chain every spring carries the whole weight, so each stretches 4 cm and the three stretches add up to 12 cm.
